title: How living things grow
source: DeepKids Combined. Covers Cambridge Stage 2 Biology Unit 4.2 'Growing' (young animals and humans change as they grow into adults; stages of human growth; measuring height). No textbook needed.
summary: Your child is about 1 cm taller in the morning than at bedtime, and finds out why by measuring. They measure height with bottles, hand spans and centimetres, and learn that bones grow longer at growth plates near their ends. They compare a butterfly's life cycle with a grasshopper's, find out why crabs and snakes must shed their outer layer to grow, and compare lifespans, from a mayfly's single day as an adult to a Greenland shark's centuries. Last, they ask why human children stay children for so long, and who helps raise them.
subconcepts: growing means getting bigger and changing shape
life cycles: birth, growth, adulthood, young of their own, and the end of life
complete metamorphosis: egg, larva, pupa, adult
incomplete metamorphosis: egg, nymph, adult (grasshoppers, cockroaches, dragonflies)
moulting: animals with a hard outer skeleton shed it to grow
stages of human growth and growth spurts
measuring growth fairly: non-standard units and centimetres
bones grow at growth plates, then stop
body proportions change as we grow
what growing needs: food, water, sleep, exercise and care
some living things keep growing all their lives
lifespans differ hugely, from a day to centuries
the long human childhood and shared care (the grandmother idea)
builds_on: Class 1: all animals have young; baby names; eggs or born alive; babies that look different (tadpoles, caterpillars); many ways of caring. This rung adds measuring, growth plates, two kinds of metamorphosis, moulting, lifespans and the long human childhood. Genes and inheriting features (also Class 2) explain why young look like their parents. Later: the human body, and how life changes over very long times.
goals: By the end your child can measure a person's height fairly with non-standard units and in centimetres, and record it in a block graph.
By the end your child can describe the stages of a human life and say how a body changes as it grows (height, proportions, teeth).
By the end your child can compare a butterfly's life cycle with a grasshopper's, and explain why some animals moult.
By the end your child can name what a body needs to grow well, including sleep.
By the end your child can give examples of animals with very short and very long lives, and of living things that never stop growing.
By the end your child can give a reason why human children need looking after for so long.
words: the stages a living thing goes through, from egg, seed or baby to an adult who has young of their own
the young stage of an insect that looks nothing like the adult, like a caterpillar or a maggot
the resting stage when a larva changes into an adult; a butterfly's pupa is a chrysalis
a young insect that looks like a small adult without wings, like a baby grasshopper
to shed an old hard skin or shell in order to grow bigger
a growing layer of soft bone near each end of a long bone in children
a small standard unit for measuring length, written cm
how long a living thing usually lives
a time of growing very fast, as in the teenage years

days.title: How tall am I?
days.goal: Remember Class 1, then measure height in different ways.

steps.title: Remember
steps.do: Quick quiz from Class 1. Ask: 'What is a baby goat called?' (A kid.) 'A baby frog?' (A tadpole.) 'Which hatches from an egg, a crocodile or a cow?' (The crocodile.) 'What are the four stages of a butterfly's life?' (Egg, caterpillar, chrysalis, butterfly.) If you made the Class 1 growing-up book, look at it, and at the height mark on the door frame. Say: 'This year we will measure how we grow.'

steps.title: Bottles, hands and centimetres
steps.do: Do Experiment e1. Your child lies on the floor with feet against a wall. Measure them with two identical water bottles laid end over end, then with your hand spans. Before using their hand spans, ask: 'Will your hands give the same number as mine? Why?' Then measure with their hand spans. Write each answer. Ask: 'Why did we get two different hand-span answers for the same height?' (Our hands are different sizes.) 'What do we need so everyone gets the same answer?' (A unit that is the same size for everyone.) Then measure with a tape in centimetres. Say: 'A centimetre is the same length everywhere: in Chennai, in Ghana, in Norway.'

steps.title: Height and age
steps.do: Measure 3–5 family members or neighbours in centimetres, standing against a wall with a book flat on their head. Your child writes name, age and height in a table, and makes a block graph on squared paper, one column per person, 1 square for 10 cm. Ask: 'What pattern do you see?' (Older children are taller, and grown-ups stop getting taller.) 'Is the oldest person the tallest?' (Not always: grown-ups stop growing, and some older people even get a little shorter.)

days.title: Where growing happens
days.goal: Find out how bones grow and how body shapes change.

steps.title: Morning height
steps.do: Experiment e2, part two. Last night at bedtime you marked your child's height and wrote down their guess. This morning, before breakfast, measure again in exactly the same way and mark the wall. Compare the two marks. Ask: 'Were you taller at bedtime or now? Was your guess right?' Don't explain yet: you will talk about why tomorrow.

steps.title: Growth plates
steps.do: Show a picture of a child's hand X-ray (search 'child hand X-ray growth plate'), or draw a long bone. First ask: 'Where in a bone do you think the growing happens?' Then say: 'Near each end of your long bones is a growing layer called a growth plate. It keeps making new bone, so your arms and legs get longer. In the late teens or early twenties the growth plates turn to hard bone and close. Then you stop getting taller.' Ask: 'Which bones grow most to make you taller?' (The leg bones and the spine.) 'Do grown-ups' bones still grow?' (Not longer. But they keep repairing and renewing themselves all through life.) Then tell your child about voice v4, Rita Levi-Montalcini, who studied how nerves grow in a laboratory she built in her bedroom, and later found one of the body's growth messengers. Ask the voice's question.

steps.title: Heads and bodies
steps.do: Do Activity a1. First ask: 'Which part of you do you think has grown most since you were a baby?' Then count how many heads tall a baby, your child and a grown-up are, using real people or full-length photos and a paper strip as long as each one's head. A newborn is about 4 heads tall, a 7-year-old about 6, and a grown-up about 7 to 8. Ask: 'So which parts grew most after birth?' (The legs and body. The head is already big at birth, because the brain grows so early.)

need: photos of a baby, your child and a grown-up

prep.task: At bedtime, measure your child's height (Experiment e2, steps 1 and 2). Ask: 'Will you be taller, shorter or the same in the morning?' Write down their guess.

days.title: Big changes and small changes
days.goal: Compare complete and incomplete metamorphosis, and find out why animals moult.

steps.title: Morning or bedtime?
steps.do: Remember Experiment e2: your child was taller in the morning than at bedtime, usually by about 1 cm. Ask: 'Did you shrink during the day? Why do you think that happened?' Listen to the idea. Then explain: between the bones of your spine are soft pads called discs. All day, standing and sitting, your body's weight presses them a little flatter. At night, lying down, they soak up fluid and spring back.

steps.title: Two ways to grow up
steps.do: Draw two life cycles side by side. Butterfly: egg, larva (caterpillar), pupa (chrysalis), adult. Grasshopper: egg, nymph, bigger nymph, adult with wings. Say: 'Metamorphosis means a big change of body shape. A butterfly changes completely on the way: this is complete metamorphosis. A young grasshopper, called a nymph, already looks like a small grasshopper without wings: this is incomplete metamorphosis.' Then sort aloud. Complete: mosquito (larvae wriggle in water, then a pupa, then the adult), housefly (a larva called a maggot, then a pupa), ladybird. Incomplete: cockroach, and dragonfly (the nymph lives underwater). Ask: 'A caterpillar eats leaves and a butterfly drinks nectar from flowers. How does that help them?' (The young and the adults don't compete for the same food.)

steps.title: The skin that gets too tight
steps.do: Ask: 'When your clothes get too small, you get new ones. What do you think a crab does when their shell gets too small?' Listen to the guess. Then say: 'Insects, crabs and spiders have a hard skeleton on the outside of their body, called an exoskeleton. It cannot stretch. So to grow, they moult. They make a new soft skin underneath, split the old one, climb out, swell up, and then the new skin hardens. Snakes shed the thin outer layer of their skin in one piece too.' Show a picture of a shed snake skin or a cicada's empty shell (search 'cicada moult'). Ask: 'Why must a crab hide just after moulting?' (The new shell is soft, so the crab is easy to eat.) 'Do you moult?' (Not all at once. Your skin grows with you, and you lose tiny flakes of it every day.) Then act it out: your child pulls on an old T-shirt that is too small, wriggles slowly out of it, takes big breaths to 'swell', and stands still while the new shell 'hardens'.

need: a picture of a shed snake skin or cicada shell, and an old T-shirt that is too small

days.title: Teeth, and the crab who had to be soft
days.goal: Count teeth, read the story and check the main ideas.

steps.title: Count your teeth
steps.do: Your child counts their teeth in a mirror, top and bottom. Say: 'Children have 20 milk teeth. From about age 6 they fall out one by one, and bigger adult teeth come up in their place. Grown-ups can have up to 32.' Ask: 'Why do you think milk teeth are replaced?' (The jaw grows bigger and needs more teeth that are bigger and stronger.) 'Is a lost tooth a sign of growing?' (Yes.)

steps.title: Story: The Crab Who Had to Be Soft
steps.do: Read the story aloud (Story tab), then ask the questions after it. Listen for the moment Kayal's mother says: 'It's not a dead crab. It's an empty coat.'

steps.title: Core worksheet
steps.do: Your child does Worksheet ws1 (core). Read each item aloud if needed. Mark it together. For each mistake, go back to the day it came from and look again.

days.title: What growing needs
days.goal: Find out what a body needs to grow well, and how scientists check growth.

steps.title: Growing foods
steps.do: Ask your child what they ate yesterday. Say: 'Your body builds new bone, muscle and blood out of your food.' Sort the foods into three groups. Body-building foods have protein: dal, sambar, chana, milk, curd, eggs, fish, meat and nuts. Energy foods: rice, idli, dosa, roti and potato. Protective foods: fruit and vegetables. Ask: 'Which foods build strong bones?' (Foods with calcium: milk, curd, ragi and green leafy vegetables.)

steps.title: Sleep and play
steps.do: Ask: 'When do you think you grow most: when you are awake or asleep?' Then say: 'Much of your growing happens while you sleep. In deep sleep your body sends out a chemical messenger called growth hormone, which tells your bones and muscles to grow.' Ask: 'How many hours did you sleep last night?' Children your age need about 9 to 12 hours. Then add the other things growing needs. Running, jumping and playing make bones and muscles strong. Water matters, because your body is more than half water. And care from people who love you matters too.

steps.title: Voice v2: who was measured?
steps.do: Tell voice v2: the World Health Organization measured healthy children in six countries, including India, to make growth charts. Show the growth chart on your child's health card if it has one. Ask the voice's question. Then ask: 'If you measured only rich children, or only children from one country, would the chart be fair to everyone?'

need: your child's health card or growth chart, if you have one

days.title: A day or four hundred years
days.goal: Compare lifespans and meet living things that never stop growing.

steps.title: Who lives longest?
steps.do: Ask your child to guess and put in order, shortest life to longest: a mouse, a dog, a human, an elephant, a tortoise. Write the guesses.

steps.title: Lifespans
steps.do: Give the real numbers. These are usual lifespans, and some live longer: a mouse about 2 years, a dog 10 to 15, an elephant 60 to 70, a human 70 to 80 or more, and a giant tortoise more than 100, sometimes over 150. Ask: 'How close were your guesses?' Then the surprises. An adult mayfly lives about a day, but before that the mayfly spent many months, often a year, as a nymph underwater. A bristlecone pine tree in the USA is more than 4,000 years old. Then tell voice v3, about the Greenland shark, and ask the voice's question. Say: 'Trees and many fish, including sharks, keep growing slowly all their lives. People and dogs stop.'

steps.title: Life Cycle Families
steps.do: Play the card game g1. Each player collects whole life cycles: butterfly, frog, grasshopper, human, mango and hen. When someone completes a family, they lay it down and say the stages aloud in order.

days.title: Why such a long childhood?
days.goal: Ask why human children grow so slowly, and who helps them.

steps.title: Who looked after you?
steps.do: Ask: 'Who has looked after you since you were born?' Write every name your child can think of: parents, grandparents, aunts and uncles, older cousins, neighbours, a teacher, the doctor, the vegetable seller who gives you a free carrot. Count them. Say: 'A whole crowd of people helped you grow.'

steps.title: Voice v1: the grandmothers
steps.do: Compare: a calf walks within an hour of birth. Baby sea turtles crawl to the sea and swim alone on their first night. A human baby can't walk for about a year, and needs looking after for more than 10 years. Ask: 'Why do you think human children grow up so slowly?' (One idea: a big brain takes years to grow, and to learn language, skills and stories.) Then tell voice v1, Kristen Hawkes and the grandmother idea, and the scientists who disagree. Ask the voice's question.

steps.title: Stretch worksheet
steps.do: Your child does Worksheet ws2 (stretch). Let them think aloud. Praise any answer with a reason.

days.title: Family growth wall and teach it back
days.goal: Finish the project, try the challenge and teach what you know.

steps.title: Project: Family Growth Wall
steps.do: Finish the project: a strip of chart paper on the wall from the floor up, with a line and name for each person measured on Day 1, the Class 1 door-frame mark if you have it, and a drawing of each person's life stage. Add today's height for your child. Ask: 'How much have you grown since the Class 1 mark?'

steps.title: Challenge worksheet
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws3 (challenge) together. Scribe the long answers. There is no single right answer for the last questions; ask 'What is your evidence?'

steps.title: Teach it back
steps.do: Your child stands by the growth wall and teaches the family: how to measure fairly, where bones grow, two kinds of metamorphosis, why crabs moult, what growing needs, and why humans have a long childhood. Ask the check questions.

sections.p: Which is the right order for a human life?
Match the young to the adult.
A butterfly's pupa is called a ____.
Why is a centimetre better than a hand span for measuring?
opts: it is the same for everyone

sections.p: Lakshmi is 118 cm tall. Kavya is 124 cm tall. Who is taller, and by how much?
You measured in the morning and again at bedtime. At bedtime you were…
Children have ____ milk teeth.
Where in your bones does growing happen?
opts: in the growth plates near the ends

sections.p: Why does a crab have to moult to grow, when you don't?
Name three things your body needs to grow well, and say why one of them matters.
Does the young look nothing like the adult (complete), or like a small adult without wings (incomplete)?
Which of these must moult to grow?
Short life or long life?
cats: short: days to a few years

sections.p: Stops growing when grown up, or keeps growing slowly all its life?
How long a living thing usually lives is its ____.
A newborn is about 4 heads tall, and a grown-up about 7 or 8. So as you grow…
opts: your legs and body grow more than your head

sections.p: A family measured only the children in one rich school to make a growth chart for all children. What's the problem?
opts: those children might not be like all children

sections.p: A calf walks an hour after it is born. A human baby takes about a year. Give one reason why.
Plan a fair test: does your little cousin grow more in a year than you do? What will you measure, how, and when?
An astronaut comes back from months in space a few centimetres taller. Why?
opts: with no gravity squashing them, the pads in the spine spread out

sections.p: An adult mayfly lives for only about a day. Does a mayfly have a short life?
opts: no, the mayfly first lived for months, often a year, as a nymph
yes, mayflies have no young stage

sections.p: Scientists worked out a Greenland shark's age by testing…
opts: the centre of the eye lens, which formed before the shark was born

sections.p: Match the puzzle to its answer.
pairs: the new shell is still soft
the jaw grows and needs bigger teeth
growth hormone is sent out in deep sleep

sections.p: Put these in order from shortest to longest lifespan: dog, elephant, mouse, giant tortoise.
An insect that hatches looking like a small wingless adult is called a ____.
Some scientists think grandmothers helped humans have long childhoods. Others think big brains and learning matter more. What evidence would help you decide?
Would you like to stay a child for longer, or grow up faster, like a calf? What would you gain and lose?
A tree keeps growing all its life. Is there anything in you that keeps growing even after you stop getting taller?

experiments.title: Bottles, hands and centimetres
experiments.question: How can we measure height so everyone gets the same answer?
need: a wall and a flat floor
steps: Your child lies flat on the floor with feet against the wall.

Lay one bottle on its side with its base touching the wall. Put the second bottle end to end with it. Then move the first bottle to the far end, and so on, up to the top of the head. Count the bottles and leave no gaps.
Write: 'I am __ bottles long.'
Now measure the same length with your hand spans, then with your child's hand spans. Write both.
Finally measure with the tape in centimetres.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Will hand spans give the same number for your hands and mine?'
experiments.observe: The bottle count comes out the same each time if done carefully. The two hand-span counts are different. The tape gives one exact number in centimetres.
experiments.why: A measurement is a count of units. If the unit changes size, as hands do, the count changes. Bottles work if everyone uses the same kind of bottle. That is why the world agreed on standard units like the centimetre. To measure carefully, leave no gaps or overlaps, start at zero, and check twice.

experiments.title: Taller in the morning
experiments.question: Are you the same height all day?
need: a pencil and a wall you can mark lightly (or a paper strip stuck to it)
steps: At bedtime, your child stands barefoot against the wall, heels touching it, looking straight ahead.
Lay the book flat on their head against the wall and mark the wall. Measure in cm.
Next morning, before breakfast and before walking around much, do exactly the same.
Compare the two marks.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Will you be taller, shorter or the same in the morning?'
experiments.observe: Usually about 1 cm taller in the morning than at bedtime.
experiments.why: Between the bones of your spine are soft, springy pads called discs. All day, standing and sitting, your body's weight presses them a little flatter, so you lose a little height. Lying down at night, they soak up fluid and spring back. Astronauts in space, where nothing presses the discs, grow a few centimetres taller for a while. It is a good lesson for scientists too: the time when you measure can change your answer.
experiments.time: 7 min at bedtime + 7 min next morning

activities.title: Heads and bodies
need: photos of a baby, your child and a grown-up, or the real people
steps: Cut a paper strip as long as the person's head (chin to top).
Lay the strip again and again from the top of the head to the feet, counting how many 'heads' tall they are.
Do it for a baby (a photo works), your child and a grown-up.
Write the three numbers and draw three stick people with the right number of heads.
Talk about which parts grew most.
activities.outcome: Three stick people showing that a baby is about 4 heads tall and a grown-up about 7 to 8: bodies don't just get bigger, they change shape.

project.title: Family Growth Wall
steps: Day 1: measure 3–5 people in cm and write the results in a table.
Day 8: stick a long strip of chart paper on the wall from the floor.
Mark each person's height with a line, their name and age.
Draw each one's life stage next to their line (child, teenager, adult, older person).
Add your child's Class 1 height mark if you have it, and today's height, and work out how much they have grown.
Leave room to add next year's mark.
project.outcome: A wall chart of growth in centimetres that the family can add to every year.

game.title: Life Cycle Families
rules: Cut out the 24 cards: six families of four. Shuffle and deal 4 cards to each player; put the rest face down.
On your turn, ask any player for a card you need: 'Do you have the frog's tadpole?' If they have it, they give it to you and you ask again. If not, take a card from the pile.
When you have all four cards of a family, lay them down in order and say the stages aloud.
The player with the most families when the cards run out wins.

cards.front: Frog 3: froglet with a little tail
Mango 4: tree with flowers and fruit

big: Why do humans have such a long childhood, when a calf walks in an hour?
If a crab sheds its whole shell, is the new crab the same crab?
Is it better to live a short, busy life like a mayfly or a long, slow one like a Greenland shark?
When do you stop growing? Do you ever stop growing in your mind?
Who should decide what 'normal' growth is for a child?

challenge.hint: They stop getting taller when their growth plates close, but their bodies keep making new skin, blood and bone to repair themselves every day, hair and nails keep growing, and their brains keep learning. What does 'grow' mean to you?

challenge.q: 'Eat your vegetables and you'll grow tall like your uncle.' Does food decide how tall you get?
challenge.hint: Partly. Children who don't get enough food grow less, and that is a big problem in the world. But how tall you can grow also depends on what you inherit from your parents. Food and family both matter. How could you find out which matters more?

challenge.q: 'Survival of the fittest' means animals must compete to survive. Is that how children grow up?
challenge.hint: Growing up is mostly about care and cooperation: parents, grandparents, aunts, older siblings and neighbours sharing the work, in humans, elephants and many birds. Competition is real too, but it is not the whole story.

perspectives.view: A crab must climb out of their old shell to grow, and then stays soft and in danger for a few days. Ask: what have you grown out of, like shoes or clothes? What is the same about a crab's moult, and what is different?

perspectives.who: An Anganwadi worker in an Indian village
perspectives.view: Anganwadi workers weigh and measure small children every month and mark their growth charts, to spot early when a child is not getting enough food. Ask: why might measuring help a child? What else would you need besides a chart?
In many Indian families grandparents help raise children: oiling hair, telling stories, cooking, teaching songs. Ask an older person in your family: who helped raise you, and what did they teach you?

voices.who: Kristen Hawkes, an American anthropologist, and the 'grandmother hypothesis'
voices.idea: Hawkes and her colleagues studied the Hadza, a people in Tanzania who gather wild foods. They saw that older women spent hours digging up tubers, and that their grandchildren gained weight better with this help. In the late 1990s they proposed that grandmothers helping to feed grandchildren may be part of why humans live long after having children, why human mothers can have babies closer together, and why human childhoods are so long.
voices.then: Many scientists found the idea exciting; others argued that hunting by men, or the need for big brains and long learning, explains our long childhood better.
voices.now: It is still debated. Most agree that humans raise children cooperatively, with many helpers, far more than other apes do. How much grandmothers in particular shaped human evolution is not settled.
voices.ask: How would you test whether grandmothers help children grow? What would you measure, and in whom?

voices.who: The World Health Organization's growth study (1997–2003), with children in Brazil, Ghana, India, Norway, Oman and the USA
voices.idea: Scientists measured thousands of healthy, well-fed young children in six very different countries, including children in Delhi. They found that babies and toddlers everywhere grow in a very similar way when they are healthy and well fed. In 2006 the WHO turned the results into growth charts for children under five, now used in India too.
voices.then: Some doctors argued that children from different places naturally grow differently, so one chart cannot fit all; others said the study showed that most differences come from food and health, not from where you are born.
voices.now: Most experts accept the charts for young children. For older children and teenagers there is more argument, and Indian doctors made separate Indian charts for ages 5 to 18 in 2015. Who is measured shapes what 'normal' looks like.
voices.ask: If you were making a growth chart, which children would you measure, and why? Who might be left out?

voices.who: Julius Nielsen and colleagues (2016), Denmark, and the Greenland shark
voices.idea: Greenland sharks grow less than 1 cm a year in the cold, dark Arctic sea. Nobody knew their age, so the team carbon-dated the centre of the shark's eye lens, which forms before birth and never changes afterwards. They estimated that the largest shark they studied was at least 272 years old, and probably around 400.
voices.then: It made the Greenland shark the longest-lived animal with a backbone known. Some scientists pointed out that the range of possible ages is very wide.
voices.now: Scientists accept that these sharks live for centuries, though the exact ages are uncertain and more work is being done.
voices.ask: The scientists couldn't watch a shark for 400 years. How did they work out the shark's age? What makes you trust (or doubt) a clever method like that?

voices.who: Rita Levi-Montalcini (1909–2012), Italy and the USA
voices.idea: When Mussolini's 1938 racial laws barred Jewish scientists from universities, Levi-Montalcini set up a laboratory in her bedroom and studied how nerves grow in chick embryos, using sewing needles as tools. Later, in the USA in the 1950s, she and Stanley Cohen discovered nerve growth factor (NGF), a chemical messenger that tells nerve cells to grow and where to go.
voices.then: Many scientists doubted for years that a single chemical could guide growth like this; some thought her results were a mistake.
voices.now: Accepted. She and Cohen shared the Nobel Prize in 1986, and many other growth factors, the body's 'grow here' messages, are now known. She kept working until she was over 100.
voices.ask: She did important science in a bedroom, with sewing needles, when she was banned from universities. What do you think a scientist really needs?

story.title: The Crab Who Had to Be Soft
text: I live in the mud of a mangrove creek at Pichavaram, on the coast of Tamil Nadu, where the trees stand on tiptoe on their roots. Twice a day the tide comes in and covers my home, and twice a day it goes out and leaves the mud shining. I am a mud crab. I have ten legs, two of them with strong claws, and a shell as hard as a pot.
For a long time my shell was my whole world. Inside it I was safe from the herons with their spear beaks, and the fish that snap, and the monitor lizards that dig. I loved my shell.

But I was growing. Every day I ate, little snails, dead fish, bits of whatever the tide brought, and every day there was more of me. And my shell did not grow. It cannot. It is not alive in the way my soft body is. It is a hard coat that my body made, and once it is made, it stays the size it is.
So my shell began to pinch. First at the edges, then everywhere. I felt squeezed when I walked. I felt squeezed when I rested in my burrow.

On the bank above the creek lived a girl called Kayal. She came down to the water most afternoons, to wash pots, or to look for crabs' holes with a stick, or just to sit. Her school shoes were tied around her neck by their laces because they were too small now, and they hurt her feet, and her mother had said there would be new ones after the harvest.

One afternoon I felt it: the time had come. Underneath my old shell, slowly, over many days, my body had already made a new one, soft and folded and wrinkled like a wet cloth. Now I drank in water until I swelled. There was a crack along the back of my old shell. The crack widened.
And I backed out.

It is the hardest thing a crab ever does. I pulled my legs out of my old legs, every one, ten of them. I pulled my claws out through the narrow joints of my old claws. I even pulled out the thin coverings of my eyes and the linings of my gills. It took a long time. When I was finally out, I was soft. Soft all over, like a ripe mango. I couldn't pinch. I couldn't run fast. Anything could have eaten me.
I crept into the deepest corner of my burrow, under a mangrove root, and waited, and swelled, and was afraid.
Kayal found my old shell the next day.
She found it lying on the mud at low tide: a whole crab, perfect, with all ten legs and both claws and even little eye cups. She picked it up and it was so light. She looked inside and it was empty.
"Amma!" Kayal cried, running up the bank with it held out in both hands. "Amma, a crab has died! There's nothing left of it!"
Her mother was spreading rice to dry on a mat. She wiped her hands on her sari and took the shell and turned it over, very carefully.

"Look," she said. "Look here, at the back." There was the long split where I had climbed out. "And look, it's not broken anywhere else. Nothing ate this crab. It's not a dead crab, Kayal. It's an empty coat."
Kayal stared at it. "A coat?"
"The crab grew too big for the shell," said her mother. "So the crab climbed out. Somewhere down there the crab is hiding, soft and new and bigger, waiting for the new shell to harden."
"It came out of all of it? Even the legs?"
"Even the legs."
Kayal held the empty shell for a long time. Then she looked down at the school shoes hanging round her neck. Last year they had been too big, and she had stuffed paper in the toes.
She didn't say anything. She just went back down to the creek, and put my old shell on a flat stone by the water, carefully, the right way up, and sat beside it until the tide began to come in.

Down in my burrow, I was hardening. It took days. My new shell turned from soft to leathery to hard, and it was bigger, so much bigger, with room inside to grow. One evening I came out into the low tide light and walked across the mud, slowly, then faster, and nothing pinched at all.
On a flat stone at the edge of the water there was an old crab shell, just my size, the size I used to be. A girl was sitting next to it with her chin on her knees, watching the water come in.
She saw me. She didn't move. And I didn't run.
story.epiphany: Animals with a hard outside, like crabs, insects and spiders, must moult to grow. The shell can't grow, so the crab makes a new soft one underneath, climbs out of the old one, swells, and waits for the new shell to harden. The turn is Kayal's mother saying 'It's not a dead crab. It's an empty coat.' Kayal's too-small shoes show the same idea without anyone saying it.
ask: Why couldn't the crab's shell grow with the crab?
Why did Kayal think the crab had died? What showed her mother it hadn't?
Why did the crab hide after moulting?
What was the same about the crab's shell and Kayal's shoes?
Why do you think Kayal put the shell on the stone and waited?

ideas.idea: Growing is changing, not just getting bigger.
ideas.more: Bodies change shape (a baby is about 4 heads tall, a grown-up 7 to 8), milk teeth are replaced, and caterpillars become butterflies. Show the heads-and-bodies stick people next to the life-cycle cards.

ideas.idea: Things with a hard outside must leave it to grow.
ideas.more: Crabs, insects and spiders moult their hard outer skeleton, and snakes shed the outer layer of their skin. A shed skin is an empty copy of the animal.
Human children grow slowly and need years of care from many people. Count the people who helped your child grow, and ask who the child helps.

unknowns: What exactly tells growth plates when to stop? Scientists know many of the messengers involved, but not the whole story of why one person stops at 150 cm and another at 190 cm.
Why do some animals, like the Greenland shark or some tortoises, live for centuries while others live a few years? Nobody fully knows.
Why did humans evolve such a long childhood? Grandmothers, big brains, learning and cooperation are all ideas, and the argument is not finished.

books.title: From Tadpole to Frog
books.author: Wendy Pfeffer
books.why: A Let's-Read-and-Find-Out book following a frog's whole life cycle in clear steps.

books.title: A Butterfly Is Patient
books.author: Dianna Hutts Aston and Sylvia Long
books.why: Beautiful, accurate paintings of caterpillars, chrysalises and butterflies, from the makers of 'An Egg Is Quiet'.

books.title: Summer Birds: The Butterflies of Maria Merian
books.author: Margarita Engle
books.why: The true story of Maria Merian, who raised caterpillars and showed that butterflies and moths hatch from eggs, when many people thought insects came from mud.

books.title: Mothers and Others: The Evolutionary Origins of Mutual Understanding
books.author: Sarah Blaffer Hrdy
books.why: A scientist's case that humans evolved to raise children together, with grandmothers and many helpers.

check.q: Why do we measure height in centimetres and not hand spans?
check.a: A centimetre is the same for everyone; hand spans are different sizes.

check.q: Where in your bones does growing happen, and when does it stop?
check.a: At the growth plates near the ends of the bones. They close in the late teens or early twenties.

check.q: How is a grasshopper's life cycle different from a butterfly's?
check.a: A young grasshopper is a nymph that looks like a small adult without wings (incomplete metamorphosis). A caterpillar changes completely inside a pupa (complete metamorphosis).
Their hard shell can't grow, so the crab climbs out of it and grows a bigger one.

check.q: Name three things your body needs to grow well.
check.a: For example: food with protein and calcium, water, sleep, exercise and care.

check.q: Name a living thing that keeps growing all their life, and one with a very long lifespan.
check.a: For example, a tree or a shark keeps growing all their life. A Greenland shark or a giant tortoise lives a very long time.

check.q: Give one reason human children need looking after for so long.
check.a: For example: a big brain takes years to grow and to learn, and humans raise children with many helpers.
